fatal_errors: The proposed dominant interphase-galvanic mechanism is not supported by the target results, which instead attribute the temperature dependence to competition among depassivation, repassivation, tribo-layer stability, abrasion, and oxide-layer fracture.
The prediction misses the nonmonotonic temperature response: degradation was minimized near 50 °C and increased at 100 °C, rather than simply increasing with elevated temperature.
The proposed single-phase-HEA baseline does not reconstruct the matched DS2205 comparator and would confound phase count with composition, hardness, microstructure, and passive-film chemistry.
No test-specific conditions are defined, including water chemistry, temperatures, load, frequency, stroke, counter-body, immersion protocol, or thermal-shock history.
The hypothesis predicts comparatively poor multiphase-HEA performance, whereas AlCoCrFeNi2.1 showed roughly an order-of-magnitude lower and more stable wear rates than DS2205.
explanation: The answer addresses tribocorrosion and invokes passive-film rupture, which has limited overlap with the high-temperature regime observed in the target. However, it incorrectly makes galvanic coupling between phases the primary cause and omits the transition from abrasion at 25 °C to polishing and minimum wear at 50 °C, followed by unstable oxidative or third-body wear at 100 °C. Its experiment is only weakly discriminating because an unrelated single-phase alloy cannot isolate galvanic coupling; phase-resolved electrochemical measurements or modification of phase spacing while holding chemistry and mechanical properties controlled would be needed. E3 supports temperature-dependent film instability in the same nominal alloy, but under chloride-containing sulfuric acid rather than deionized-water tribocorrosion. E1 concerns different HEA coatings and E2 provides little direct support. Boundaries and quantitative wear, corrosion, friction, and repassivation predictions are absent.
